one_liner: Tiny multiply-free 64-bit ARX hash; its v0.2 beat xxHash64 bulk speed in rurban/smhasher, current v0.3 does not.
what_it_does: pengyhash is a seeded 64-bit non-cryptographic hash for byte buffers: one C function, uint64_t pengyhash(const void *p, size_t size, uint64_t seed), in a 36-line .c file plus a header. It is a one-shot API only, with no streaming or incremental state. Two versions are in circulation with different outputs. v0.2 (2020) is BSD-2-Clause, takes a 32-bit seed and is the one bundled in rurban/smhasher and the Fortran stdlib. v0.3 (Nov 2022, the current repo) is GPLv3 and takes a 64-bit seed.
how_it_is_fast: It uses no multiplications. The state is four 64-bit words updated with add-rotate-xor (ARX) steps, 32 input bytes per iteration, in two cross-coupled chains (s0/s1 and s2/s3), with every input word added twice per block. The last 0-31 bytes are packed into four words and mixed by six fixed finalization rounds, the only place the seed enters. There is no SIMD; speed comes from cheap scalar ALU ops and instruction-level parallelism.
when_to_use: You want a very small, portable 64-bit hash with no multiplies, for example on cores where 64x64 multiplication is slow. The whole algorithm is about 25 lines of add, rotate and xor.
Hashing medium-to-large buffers (KBs and up) where scalar XXH64-class throughput is enough: about 3.8 bytes/cycle for v0.3 in SMHasher3, about 4.7 for v0.2 in rurban/smhasher.

You need the same output on little- and big-endian hosts. v0.3 assembles words byte by byte in little-endian order, and SMHasher3 registers it as endian-independent with identical LE/BE verification values.
You must match hash values already produced by rurban/smhasher or the Fortran stdlib pengy_hash; that requires the v0.2 code (BSD-2-Clause), not the current repo.
when_not_to_use: Short keys such as hash-table strings or integers: SMHasher3 averages 89.81 cycles/hash on 1-31-byte keys (about 116 at 8-16 bytes), against 52.60 for XXH64 and 29.31 for wyhash. rurban/smhasher shows 74.79 vs 49.67 for xxHash64.

Expecting to beat XXH64 with the code you download today: the current v0.3 runs about 4% slower than XXH64 in SMHasher3 (12.47 vs 13.02 GiB/s). xxh3 and wyhash are about 1.6-1.7x faster in bulk in the rurban table.
Proprietary or permissively licensed products: v0.3 is GPLv3, unlike most peer non-crypto hashes. Only the older v0.2 is BSD-2-Clause.

Seeded use that relies on the seed to separate hash families. The seed is mixed in only during finalization, and SMHasher3's SeedBlockLen test finds full 64-bit collisions on 16-31-byte keys (126 found where 0 are expected) when seed and key blocks vary together.
Code that must be well-defined C: v0.3 has an unsequenced read and write of the same state word, reported in 2023 (issue #2) and unanswered, in a repo abandoned since November 2022.

integration.platforms: any (portable scalar C, no intrinsics); v0.3 output is endian-independent, v0.2 (memcpy loads) is not
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The function is pure (no globals or static state), so concurrent calls are safe by construction.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it is a one-shot (buffer, length, 64-bit seed) -> uint64_t call like one-shot XXH64, but produces different values and has no streaming API

gotchas: Undefined behavior in v0.3. Statements such as s[1] = (s[0] += (s[1] += V64(p+8)) + V64(p)) ^ rotl(s[1],14) read and modify s[1] without a sequence point (GCC -Wsequence-point), so the hash can change with the compiler's evaluation order. SMHasher3 ships a rewrite with explicit sequencing whose verification value (0x861A1254) matches the repo's own v0.3 log. Use that form.

v0.2 and v0.3 give different hashes, and the published ~19% win over xxHash64 was measured on v0.2 (rurban/smhasher bundles v0.2, verification 0x1FC2217B; v0.3 is 0x861A1254). v0.2 also reads input with native-endian memcpy, so its values differ on big-endian machines, which the Fortran stdlib documents for its port.

The license changed from BSD-2-Clause (v0.2) to GPLv3 (v0.3) in the same commit that changed the algorithm, so older attributions citing BSD for pengyhash.c at master (rurban issue #210, Fortran stdlib docs) now point at GPLv3 code.
Every call runs six full finalization rounds regardless of length, so there is a fixed ~68-116-cycle cost per hash even for 1-byte keys (SMHasher3: 67.63 cycles at 1 byte).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Rarely. SpookyHash (SpookyV2_64) matches its rurban bulk speed (13,401 vs 13,347 MiB/s), and xxHash (XXH3) and wyhash are about 1.6-1.7x faster in bulk and much faster on short keys, so pengyhash only wins if a tiny multiply-free ARX hash with endian-independent output (v0.3) is itself the requirement.
verified_claims_summary: rurban/smhasher's 262,144-byte bulk test on its reference Ryzen 5 3350G (logs normalized to 3 GHz; compiler and flags unstated) measured pengyhash v0.2 at 13,347 MiB/s against 11,177 MiB/s for xxHash64. That is ~19%, or ~9% against xxHash64's best alignment (12,263 MiB/s), since xxHash64 drops to 10,125 MiB/s at alignments 4-7. SMHasher3 on a Ryzen 9 3950X pinned at 3.5 GHz measured the current v0.3 at 12.47 GiB/s vs 13.02 GiB/s for XXH64, about 4% slower.
status_note: Abandoned: the last commit (v0.3 and the GPLv3 relicense) was November 2022, and a 2023 undefined-behavior report is unanswered. The two small files are trivial to vendor, but pick v0.2 (BSD-2-Clause) or SMHasher3's sequenced v0.3 rewrite deliberately, based on your license and output-compatibility needs.
